options: Both true, reason does not explain
questions.why: The correct answer is “Both true, reason explains”. Reasoning: 5 hundreds → 4 hundreds 9 tens 10 ones; 10 − 1 = 9 → 499. A choice like “Both true, reason does not explain” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: Tickets cost ₹125 for adults and ₹75 for children. Papa pays for 2 adults and 1 child with ₹500. What change does he get?
questions.why: The correct answer is “₹175”. Reasoning: 125 + 125 + 75 = 325; 500 − 325 = 175. A choice like “₹325” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

school-c3-maths-b.title: Class 3 Maths · Part B (Ch 4–6)
school-c3-maths-b.description: Class 3 Mathematics: measuring length, shapes and designs, and more addition and subtraction in daily life.

courses.title: Ch 4 · Long and Short
courses.note: Chapter names follow the Math-Magic edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Measuring length with body units, why we need standard units, centimetres and metres, and estimating lengths.
outcomes: Learners can compare lengths as longer, shorter, taller
Learners can explain why hand-spans give different answers
Learners can measure with a ruler in centimetres
Learners know 1 metre = 100 centimetres and choose the right unit

scenes.text: Papa measured a table: 8 hand-spans. Little Jia measured the same table: 12 hand-spans!
'Who is right?' asked Jia. 'Both!' laughed Papa. 'My hand is bigger than yours.'

steps.title: Body units
steps.body:
Long ago people measured with their bodies:
- **Hand-span**: tip of thumb to tip of little finger, hand stretched.
- **Cubit**: elbow to the tip of the middle finger.
- **Footstep / pace**.

These are handy but **different for different people**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A rope is 6 of Ravi's cubits and 9 of his sister's cubits. Whose cubit is longer? Fewer units cover the same length → Ravi's cubit is **longer**.

**Example 2:** Which body unit would you use to measure a pencil? A **finger width** or hand-span — footsteps are too big.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 'more units' means the object is longer. It may only mean the unit is smaller.
- Leaving gaps or overlapping when placing hand-spans.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Measure your bed in hand-spans. Ask a grown-up to do it too. Compare your numbers.

statements.s: A small child and an adult will get the same number of hand-spans for a table.
If fewer units fit, each unit is bigger.
A cubit is from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “Thumb tip to little-finger tip”. Reasoning: Stretched hand, thumb to little finger. A choice like “Head to foot” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Why do two people get different hand-span answers?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Their hands are different sizes”. Reasoning: Body units vary. A choice like “The table changes” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A room is 10 of Ali's steps and 14 of Mini's steps. Whose step is longer?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Ali's”. Reasoning: Fewer steps → longer steps. A choice like “Mini's” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Best body unit to measure a playground?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Footsteps”. Reasoning: Large lengths need bigger units. A choice like “Finger width” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: The cubit goes from elbow to…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Middle-finger tip”. Reasoning: Traditional definition. A choice like “Wrist” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Teacher gave everyone a ruler. Now everyone measured the pencil as 15 cm.
'A standard unit means everyone gets the same answer,' said Teacher.

steps.title: Standard unit: centimetre
steps.body: A **centimetre (cm)** is a small standard unit — about the width of your little fingernail. A school ruler is usually 15 cm or 30 cm long.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** An eraser starts at 0 and ends at 4. Length = **4 cm**.

**Example 2:** A crayon starts at 2 and ends at 9 on the ruler. Length = 9 − 2 = **7 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Starting at the edge of the ruler instead of the **0** mark.
- Reading the end mark when the object did not start at 0 — subtract the start.

steps.title: How to measure
steps.body:
- Place the 0 mark at one end.
- Keep the ruler straight along the object.
- Read the mark at the other end.

activity.prompt: A leaf starts at the 3 cm mark and ends at the 11 cm mark. How long is it?

quiz.q: Why do we use standard units?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Everyone gets the same answer”. Reasoning: Same unit for everyone. A choice like “They are bigger” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A stick from 0 to 12 on a ruler is…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “12 cm”. Reasoning: Read the end mark. A choice like “13 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: From 5 to 10 on a ruler is…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “5 cm”. Reasoning: 10 − 5 = 5. A choice like “10 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Where should the object start on a ruler?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “At 0”. Reasoning: Start at zero. A choice like “At the edge” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “15 cm or 30 cm”. Reasoning: Typical lengths. A choice like “1 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: The tailor measured cloth for a curtain: 2 metres.
'Why not centimetres?' asked Nisha. 'Because 200 cm is a lot to count!' smiled the tailor.

steps.title: The metre
steps.body: **1 metre (m) = 100 centimetres (cm).** A metre is about the length from your nose to the tip of a grown-up's stretched arm, or the height of a door handle from the floor (roughly).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 3 m = 3 × 100 = **300 cm**.

**Example 2:** Which unit for (a) a classroom length (b) a button? (a) **metres** (b) **centimetres**.

**Example 3:** 1 m 25 cm = 100 + 25 = **125 cm**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 1 m = 10 cm. It is **100 cm**.
- Measuring long things in cm and getting tired counting — choose metres.

steps.title: Estimating
steps.body: Guess first, then measure. Good guessers get close: a door is about 2 m tall; your notebook is about 25 cm long.

activity.prompt: Which unit would you use?

quiz.why: The correct answer is “100 cm”. Reasoning: 100 centimetres. A choice like “10 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “200 cm”. Reasoning: 2 × 100. A choice like “2000 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Best unit for a saree's length?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “m”. Reasoning: Long length → metres. A choice like “kg” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “140 cm”. Reasoning: 100 + 40. A choice like “104 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A door is about how tall?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2 m”. Reasoning: Around 2 metres. A choice like “2 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Rina's ribbon is 45 cm. Tanu's ribbon is 38 cm.
They joined them for a gift. 'How long now?' They added: 83 cm!

steps.title: Lengths are numbers too
steps.body: You can add, subtract and compare lengths — just keep the **same unit** and write it in the answer.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 45 cm + 38 cm = **83 cm**.

**Example 2:** A rope is 1 m long. 35 cm is cut off. Left? Change 1 m to 100 cm: 100 − 35 = **65 cm**.

**Example 3:** Who is taller: Asha 128 cm or Binu 1 m 20 cm? Binu = 120 cm, so **Asha** is taller.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting cm from m directly (1 − 35). Change to the same unit first.
- Forgetting to write the unit.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Measure the length of your shoe and a family member's shoe. Find the difference.

activity.prompt: A cloth is 2 m long. The tailor cuts 75 cm. How many cm are left?

quiz.why: The correct answer is “55 cm”. Reasoning: Add numbers, keep unit. A choice like “45 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “60 cm”. Reasoning: 100 − 40. A choice like “39 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Who is taller: 1 m 5 cm or 110 cm?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “110 cm”. Reasoning: 1 m 5 cm = 105 cm. A choice like “1 m 5 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Before subtracting m and cm you should…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Change to the same unit”. Reasoning: Same unit first. A choice like “Add them” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Three sticks of 20 cm each joined end to end make…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “60 cm”. Reasoning: 20+20+20. A choice like “40 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Which is longer, a pencil or a bus?
questions.why: The correct answer is “Bus”. Reasoning: A bus is many metres long. A choice like “Pencil” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “100”. Reasoning: Standard fact. A choice like “10” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Body unit”. Reasoning: It varies by person. A choice like “Weight unit” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: An eraser from 0 to 5 cm is…
questions.why: The correct answer is “5 cm”. Reasoning: Read end mark. A choice like “4 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Best unit to measure a rubber band?
questions.why: The correct answer is “cm”. Reasoning: Small object. A choice like “m” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “400 cm”. Reasoning: 4 × 100. A choice like “40 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A wall is 7 of Papa's steps and 11 of Raju's. Whose step is shorter?
questions.why: The correct answer is “Raju's”. Reasoning: More steps → shorter step. A choice like “Same” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A ribbon starts at 4 cm and ends at 13 cm. Length?
questions.why: The correct answer is “9 cm”. Reasoning: 13 − 4. A choice like “4 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “230 cm”. Reasoning: 200 + 30. A choice like “23 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “35 cm”. Reasoning: 100 − 65. A choice like “64 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “1 m 10 cm”. Reasoning: 1 m 10 cm = 110 cm. A choice like “99 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: A carpenter needs 3 pieces of wood of 40 cm each. He has a 1 m plank. Is it enough?
questions.why: The correct answer is “No, he needs 20 cm more”. Reasoning: 3 × 40 = 120 cm > 100 cm; short by 20 cm. A choice like “No, needs 40 cm more” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Assertion: Body units are good for exact measuring. Reason: Everyone's hand is the same size.
questions.why: The correct answer is “Both false”. Reasoning: Body units differ; hands vary. A choice like “Both true” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: Dhruv is 1 m 32 cm tall; his sister is 18 cm shorter. Her height?
questions.why: The correct answer is “1 m 14 cm”. Reasoning: 132 − 18 = 114 cm = 1 m 14 cm. A choice like “1 m 50 cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A frog jumps 25 cm each time. How many jumps to cover 1 m?
questions.why: The correct answer is “4”. Reasoning: 25 + 25 + 25 + 25 = 100. A choice like “5” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

courses.title: Ch 5 · Shapes and Designs
courses.note: Chapter names follow the Math-Magic edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Flat shapes and their corners and sides, straight and curved lines, tangram-style puzzles, and tiling patterns.
outcomes: Learners can name triangle, square, rectangle, circle and count sides and corners
Learners can tell straight and curved edges
Learners can build bigger shapes from smaller ones
Learners can spot shapes that tile without gaps

scenes.text: Uncle Yusuf cut paper into shapes for kites.
'This one has 3 sides, this one 4,' he said. 'And the moon one has no corners at all!'

steps.title: Common flat shapes
steps.body:
- **Triangle**: 3 sides, 3 corners.
- **Square**: 4 equal sides, 4 corners.
- **Rectangle**: 4 sides, opposite sides equal, 4 corners.
- **Circle**: 1 curved line, no corners.

A corner is where two sides meet.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** How many corners do 2 triangles and 1 square have together? 3 + 3 + 4 = **10**.

**Example 2:** A shape has 4 sides; only opposite sides are equal. It is a **rectangle**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Calling a tilted square a 'diamond' and thinking it is a new shape — it is still a square.
- Saying a circle has one corner.

steps.title: Look around
steps.body: Find shapes at home: a roti (circle), a door (rectangle), a samosa face (triangle), a chessboard box (square).

activity.prompt: Match shape and number of corners

quiz.q: A triangle has how many sides?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “3”. Reasoning: Tri = three. A choice like “2” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Circle”. Reasoning: A circle is one curved line. A choice like “Rectangle” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “4 corners”. Reasoning: Both are four-sided. A choice like “3 sides” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Still a square”. Reasoning: Turning does not change the shape. A choice like “A triangle” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “9”. Reasoning: 3 × 3. A choice like “6” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Dadi drew a rangoli with straight lines and curvy petals.
Lila traced the straight lines with a ruler and the petals with her finger.

steps.title: Two kinds of lines
steps.body:
- **Straight line**: does not bend — you can draw it with a ruler.
- **Curved line**: bends smoothly — like a rainbow or the letter C.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Letters with only straight lines: A, E, F, H, L, T. Letters with only curved lines: C, O, S.

**Example 2:** Letter D has 1 straight line and 1 curved line.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a slanting line is curved. Slanting can still be straight.
- Forgetting that some shapes mix straight and curved edges (a semicircle).

activity.prompt: Sort the letters

quiz.q: Which letter has only straight lines?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “E”. Reasoning: E is made of straight lines. A choice like “C” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A slanting line drawn with a ruler is…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Straight”. Reasoning: It doesn't bend. A choice like “Broken” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

options: One straight and one curved edge
quiz.why: The correct answer is “One straight and one curved edge”. Reasoning: Half a circle plus a straight edge. A choice like “Only straight edges” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Letter D has how many curved lines?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1”. Reasoning: One curve, one straight. A choice like “0” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Curved line”. Reasoning: It bends. A choice like “Triangle” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: A square tile broke into pieces. Arjun tried to put it back.
He made a cat, a boat and finally the square again! The same pieces made many pictures.

steps.title: Shapes join to make shapes
steps.body:
- 2 equal triangles can make a **square** or a bigger **triangle**.
- 2 equal squares side by side make a **rectangle**.
- A **tangram** is a square cut into 7 pieces (5 triangles, 1 square, 1 slanted four-sided piece) that can be arranged into many pictures.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Fold a square paper corner to corner and cut. You get **2 triangles**.

**Example 2:** How many small squares make a rectangle 3 squares long and 2 squares wide? 3 + 3 = **6**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Leaving gaps or overlaps when fitting pieces.
- Thinking pieces must be used the same way up — you may turn and flip them.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Cut a square of paper into 4 triangles by folding along both diagonals. Make a big triangle, a rectangle and a fish.

items.back: Can make a square or a bigger triangle

quiz.q: Cutting a square along one diagonal gives…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “2 triangles”. Reasoning: Corner-to-corner cut. A choice like “1 rectangle” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: 2 equal squares side by side make a…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Rectangle”. Reasoning: Twice as long as wide. A choice like “Circle” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A tangram has how many pieces?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “7”. Reasoning: Classic tangram = 7. A choice like “5” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: How many small squares in a 2 by 2 big square?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “4”. Reasoning: 2 + 2. A choice like “6” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Turn them”. Reasoning: Turning is allowed; gaps aren't. A choice like “Only use one” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Workers laid square tiles on the bathroom floor — no gaps anywhere.
Mira asked, 'Why not round tiles?' Papa drew circles: gaps appeared between them!

steps.title: Tiling
steps.body:
**Tiling** means covering a floor with shapes, with **no gaps and no overlaps**.
- Squares, rectangles, triangles and hexagons (like honeycomb) tile well.
- Circles leave gaps.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Why do bees use hexagons? Hexagons fit together with no gaps and use little wax.

**Example 2:** A floor is 5 tiles long and 4 tiles wide. Tiles needed = 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = **20**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting only the tiles on the edge instead of every row.
- Thinking any shape tiles — check for gaps.

steps.title: Look around
steps.body: Look at brick walls, footpaths and honeycombs — they are all tiling patterns.

statements.s: Circles can cover a floor without gaps.
Squares tile a floor with no gaps.
A honeycomb is made of hexagons.

quiz.q: Which shape leaves gaps when tiling?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Circle”. Reasoning: Curved edges can't fit tightly. A choice like “Triangle” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Hexagons”. Reasoning: Six-sided. A choice like “Circles” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A floor 3 tiles long and 3 wide needs…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “9”. Reasoning: 3 + 3 + 3. A choice like “3” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Tiling means no gaps and no…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Overlaps”. Reasoning: Tiles must not overlap. A choice like “Corners” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Bricks in a wall make a…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Tiling pattern”. Reasoning: Rectangles fitted together. A choice like “Clock” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A square has how many corners?
questions.why: The correct answer is “4”. Reasoning: Four. A choice like “3” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Circle”. A choice like “Square” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks. Read the question again and test each choice before you decide.
The correct answer is “A curved line”. Reasoning: A loop. A choice like “Straight lines” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: How many sides do a triangle and a rectangle have together?
questions.why: The correct answer is “7”. Reasoning: 3 + 4. A choice like “5” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Which letter has both straight and curved lines?
questions.why: The correct answer is “P”. Reasoning: P has a straight stem and a curve. A choice like “L” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Square”. Reasoning: Join along the long side. A choice like “Hexagon only” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Hexagon”. Reasoning: Hexagons fit without gaps. A choice like “Oval” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A shape with 4 equal sides is a…
questions.why: The correct answer is “Square”. Reasoning: Definition of square. A choice like “Rectangle” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “12”. Reasoning: 4 × 3 = 12. A choice like “8” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A floor is 6 tiles long, 2 tiles wide. Tiles?
questions.why: The correct answer is “12”. Reasoning: 6 + 6. A choice like “8” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Which is NOT true about a rectangle?

courses.title: Ch 6 · Fun with Give and Take
courses.note: Chapter names follow the Math-Magic edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Using addition and subtraction in everyday life: number patterns, estimating, missing numbers, and keeping score.
outcomes: Learners can find missing numbers in addition and subtraction
Learners can estimate sums and differences by rounding to tens

scenes.text: A shop bill got wet: 'Rice ₹__ + Dal ₹85 = ₹230'.
Neel became a detective: 230 − 85 = 145. 'Rice cost ₹145!'

steps.title: Addition and subtraction are partners
steps.body: If **a + b = c**, then **c − b = a** and **c − a = b**. Use the opposite operation to find a missing number.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- In ___ − 46 = 54, subtracting (54 − 46). The missing number is the **start**, so add.
- Not checking by putting the answer back.

activity.prompt: Find the missing numbers

quiz.why: The correct answer is “60”. Reasoning: 100 − 40. A choice like “40” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “50”. Reasoning: 250 − 200. A choice like “450” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “100”. Reasoning: 70 + 30. A choice like “40” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Asha had ₹100. She wanted a book for ₹48 and colours for ₹39.
'About 50 + 40 = 90. Yes, enough!' She was right: the exact total was ₹87.

steps.title: Rounding to the nearest ten
steps.body:
Look at the ones digit:
- 0–4 → round **down** (43 → 40).
- 5–9 → round **up** (48 → 50).

Estimate = add or subtract the rounded numbers.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Estimate 48 + 39 → 50 + 40 = **about 90**. Exact = 87.

**Example 2:** Estimate 92 − 37 → 90 − 40 = **about 50**. Exact = 55.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Rounding 45 down to 40. Numbers ending in 5 round **up** (45 → 50).
- Giving an estimate as the final exact answer when the question asks for the exact value.

steps.title: Why estimate?
steps.body: Estimates help you check if an exact answer is sensible, and help when shopping.

activity.prompt: Match the number with its nearest ten

steps.title: Finding the rule
steps.body: Look at how each number changes from the one before. Is something **added** or **taken away**? The same change each time is the **rule**.

steps.title: Common mistakes

- Mixing up adding and subtracting when the pattern goes down.

scenes.text: Team Blue scored 86 in the first innings and 73 in the second.

steps.title: Plan in steps
steps.body:
- Read the problem twice.
- Find what is asked.
- Do **step 1** (often a total).
- Use that answer in **step 2**.
- Check that the answer makes sense.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Blue = 86 + 73 = 159. Difference = 159 − 142 = **17**. Blue won by 17 runs.

**Example 2:** Mohan had ₹200. He bought a toy for ₹75 and a ball for ₹40. Spent = 115. Left = 200 − 115 = **₹85**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Stopping after step 1 and giving the total instead of what was asked.
- Subtracting both items from different numbers.

school-c3-maths-c.title: Class 3 Maths · Part C (Ch 7–9)
school-c3-maths-c.description: Class 3 Mathematics: time and calendars, weight, and multiplication.

courses.title: Ch 7 · Time Goes On
courses.note: Chapter names follow the Math-Magic edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Days, weeks, months and the calendar; reading a clock to the hour and half-hour; morning, afternoon and night; how long things take.
outcomes: Learners know 7 days = 1 week and 12 months = 1 year
Learners can read a calendar to find dates and days
Learners can read time to the hour, half-hour and quarter-hour
Learners can compare how long activities take

scenes.text: It was 10 May. Summer holidays began on 24 May.
Sam counted: '2 weeks to go! 14 days!' He ticked one box every night.

steps.title: Time facts
steps.body:
- 1 week = **7 days** (Monday to Sunday).
- 1 year = **12 months** (January to December).
- Months have 30 or 31 days; **February** has 28 days (29 in a leap year).
- 1 year = 365 days (366 in a leap year).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Today is Tuesday. What day is it after 7 days? 7 days = 1 week, so **Tuesday** again.

**Example 2:** Today is Friday. What day is it after 3 days? Sat (1), Sun (2), Mon (3) → **Monday**.

**Example 3:** How many days in 3 weeks? 7 + 7 + 7 = **21**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting today as day 1 when asked 'after 3 days'. Start counting from the next day.
- Thinking every month has 30 days.

steps.title: Knuckle trick
steps.body: Make a fist. Knuckles are 31-day months, gaps between them are shorter months: Jan (knuckle) 31, Feb (gap) 28/29, Mar 31, Apr 30, May 31, Jun 30, Jul 31, then start again: Aug 31, Sep 30, Oct 31, Nov 30, Dec 31.

activity.prompt: Put the months in order (first six)

quiz.q: How many days make a week?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “7”. Reasoning: Seven days. A choice like “6” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “February”. Reasoning: 28 or 29 days. A choice like “December” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Today is Sunday. After 2 days it will be…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Tuesday”. Reasoning: Mon (1), Tue (2). A choice like “Monday” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: How many months in a year?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “12”. Reasoning: Twelve. A choice like “52” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “14”. Reasoning: 7 + 7. A choice like “21” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Dadi's birthday is on 15 August, the same day as Independence Day.
Rohit found August on the calendar and moved his finger to 15. 'It's a Friday this year!'

steps.title: How a calendar page works
steps.body: Each page shows one month. Columns are days of the week. Rows are weeks. Moving **down one box** = 7 days later; moving **right one box** = 1 day later.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** If 3 March is a Monday, what day is 10 March? 10 − 3 = 7 days → **Monday**.

**Example 2:** If 3 March is a Monday, what day is 17 March? 17 − 3 = 14 = 2 weeks → **Monday**.

**Example 3:** If 1 June is a Thursday, then 4 June is Thu → Fri (2) → Sat (3) → **Sunday** (4).

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading across the wrong row.
- Forgetting that the 1st of a month need not be a Monday.

steps.title: In real life
steps.body: Calendars help plan festivals, exams, birthdays and doctor visits. Mark one special day for each month this year.

activity.prompt: If 5 July is a Wednesday, which date is the next Wednesday?

quiz.q: Moving down one box on a calendar is…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “7 days later”. Reasoning: One week. A choice like “1 month later” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: If 2 May is Saturday, 9 May is…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Saturday”. Reasoning: 7 days later. A choice like “Sunday” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: If 1 April is Tuesday, 3 April is…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Thursday”. Reasoning: Wed (2), Thu (3). A choice like “Monday” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Independence Day in India is on…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “15 August”. A choice like “2 October” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks. Read the question again and test each choice before you decide.

quiz.q: How many days does June have?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “30”. Reasoning: June has 30 days. A choice like “29” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Prayer starts when the short hand is at 9 and the long hand is at 12 — 9 o'clock.
Lunch is when the short hand is halfway between 12 and 1 and the long hand is at 6 — half past 12.

steps.title: Two hands
steps.body:
- **Short hand** = hours.
- **Long hand** = minutes.
- Long hand at **12** → o'clock.
- Long hand at **6** → half past (30 minutes).
- Long hand at **3** → quarter past (15 minutes).
- Long hand at **9** → quarter to (45 minutes past).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Short hand at 4, long hand at 12 → **4 o'clock (4:00)**.

**Example 2:** Short hand just past 7, long hand at 3 → **quarter past 7 (7:15)**.

**Example 3:** Short hand nearly at 11, long hand at 9 → **quarter to 11 (10:45)**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Mixing up the two hands.
- Reading 'quarter to 11' as 11:45. It is 15 minutes **before** 11, i.e. **10:45**.

steps.title: Facts
steps.body: 1 hour = 60 minutes. The long hand goes once around the clock in 1 hour. The short hand goes around twice in a day.

activity.prompt: Match the words with the time

quiz.why: The correct answer is “Short hand”. Reasoning: The short hand. A choice like “Both” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “half past”. Reasoning: 30 minutes. A choice like “quarter past” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “2:15”. Reasoning: 15 minutes after 2. A choice like “2:30” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “8:45”. Reasoning: 15 minutes before 9. A choice like “9:45” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “60”. Reasoning: Sixty. A choice like “100” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Brushing teeth took Nia 2 minutes. Walking to school took 20 minutes.
A bean seed took about a week to sprout. 'Some things take minutes, some take days!'

steps.title: Units of time
steps.body:
- Very short tasks: **seconds** (a clap, a blink).
- Short tasks: **minutes** (brushing, a meal).
- Longer: **hours** (school day, a train journey).
- Long: **days, months, years** (a seed growing, a baby growing).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A film starts at 3:00 and ends at 5:00. Duration = **2 hours**.

**Example 2:** Homework from 4:00 to 4:30 → **30 minutes**.

**Example 3:** Which takes longer: boiling an egg or growing a mango tree? Growing a tree takes **years**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the wrong unit ('I slept 8 minutes' instead of 8 hours).
- Counting the start hour as one hour.

The correct answer is “30 minutes”. Reasoning: Half an hour. A choice like “15 minutes” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A baby growing into a child takes…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Years”. Reasoning: Long time. A choice like “Hours” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A class runs from 9:00 to 9:45. How long?
questions.why: The correct answer is “45 minutes”. A choice like “1 hour” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks. Read the question again and test each choice before you decide.

questions.q: Which is the correct unit: 'I walked to school in 15 ___'?
questions.why: The correct answer is “minutes”. Reasoning: A walk takes minutes. A choice like “days” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.why: The correct answer is “9:30”. Reasoning: 8:00, 8:30, 9:00, 9:30. A choice like “10:00” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.why: The correct answer is “A false, R true”. Reasoning: Not always 28. A choice like “Both true” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

courses.title: Ch 8 · Who is Heavier?
courses.note: Chapter names follow the Math-Magic edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Comparing weights, using a simple balance, why big things are not always heavy, and kilograms and grams.
outcomes: Learners can compare weights using heavier, lighter, equal
Learners can read a simple balance
Learners know 1 kg = 1000 g and choose the right unit
Learners can add and compare weights

scenes.text: Bholu sat on one end of the see-saw and Golu on the other. Golu's end went down.
'The heavier side goes down!' said Bholu.

steps.title: Comparing weight
steps.body: We can feel weight by lifting things in our hands, but a **balance** is fairer: the pan with the **heavier** thing goes **down**; if both pans are level, the weights are **equal**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A pumpkin on one pan, a tomato on the other. The pumpkin side goes down → pumpkin is **heavier**.

**Example 2:** A big balloon and a small stone. Big does not mean heavy: the **stone** is heavier.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking bigger always means heavier (a pillow vs a brick).
- Reading the balance the wrong way: the **lower** pan is heavier.

steps.title: Make a balance
steps.body: Hang two cups from the ends of a hanger with string. Compare a spoon and a pencil.

statements.s: On a balance, the heavier object's pan goes down.
A big pillow is always heavier than a small brick.
If both pans are level, the weights are equal.

quiz.q: On a balance, the pan that goes down holds the…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Heavier thing”. Reasoning: Heavier sinks. A choice like “Lighter thing” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Brick”. Reasoning: A brick is dense. A choice like “Leaf” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “Equal weight”. Reasoning: Balance. A choice like “Right heavier” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Big things are always heavy. True?
quiz.why: The correct answer is “False”. Reasoning: A balloon is big but light. A choice like “True” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: On a see-saw, the end that goes down has the…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Heavier child”. Reasoning: Heavier side drops. A choice like “Lighter child” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Ammi asked for 1 kg potatoes and 250 g green chillies.
The shopkeeper used metal weights: a big 1 kg one and a small 250 g one.

steps.title: Standard units of weight
steps.body:
- **Kilogram (kg)** for heavier things: rice, potatoes, people.
- **Gram (g)** for light things: a pencil, spices, a letter.
- **1 kg = 1000 g**. Half a kg = 500 g. Quarter kg = 250 g.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 1 kg = 100 g. It is **1000 g**.
- Using kg for a pencil or g for a sack of rice.

steps.title: Fact
steps.body: A 1-litre bottle of water weighs about 1 kg.

activity.prompt: Would you weigh it in kg or g?

quiz.why: The correct answer is “1000 g”. Reasoning: Thousand grams. A choice like “500 g” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “500 g”. Reasoning: Half of 1000. A choice like “100 g” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “A pen”. Reasoning: Light object. A choice like “A sack of rice” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “3000 g”. Reasoning: 3 × 1000. A choice like “30 g” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “1 kg”. Reasoning: 1000 g = 1 kg. A choice like “500 g” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Bag rule on the bus: each child can carry at most 5 kg.
Lina's bag: clothes 2 kg, snacks 1 kg, books 1 kg 500 g. 'Total 4 kg 500 g — allowed!'

steps.title: Same unit first
steps.body: To add or compare weights, change them to the **same unit**, then add, subtract or compare.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 2 kg + 1 kg + 1 kg 500 g = 4 kg 500 g.

**Example 2:** Which is heavier: 1200 g or 1 kg? 1 kg = 1000 g, so **1200 g** is heavier.

**Example 3:** A bag of 1 kg sugar; 300 g used. Left = 1000 − 300 = **700 g**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Comparing 900 g and 1 kg by the numbers 900 and 1 only.
- Forgetting units in the answer.

activity.prompt: A 2 kg bag of flour. Mummy uses 750 g. How many grams are left?

quiz.why: The correct answer is “1 kg”. Reasoning: 1 kg = 1000 g. A choice like “Equal” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “1 kg 200 g”. Reasoning: 1200 g. A choice like “12 g” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “600 g”. Reasoning: 1000 − 400. A choice like “1400 g” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Before comparing kg and g, we…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “Change to the same unit”. Reasoning: Same unit. A choice like “Guess” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “5 kg”. Reasoning: Add. A choice like “6 kg” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: At the fair, a game asked: 'Guess the pumpkin's weight!'
Tina guessed 3 kg. It was 3 kg 200 g — closest guess won!

steps.title: Benchmarks
steps.body:
Remember some known weights:
- A 1-litre water bottle ≈ 1 kg.
- A small apple ≈ 150 g.
- A Class 3 child ≈ 20–30 kg.
Use them to guess other weights.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** About how heavy is a school bag full of books? A few water bottles → about **3 kg**.

**Example 2:** Which is a sensible weight for an egg: 50 g or 5 kg? **50 g**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Wild guesses like 'my pencil weighs 2 kg'. Compare with a benchmark first.

steps.title: Health tip
steps.body: Doctors recommend a school bag should not be too heavy for a child's back. Pack only what you need for the day.

activity.prompt: Match the object with a sensible weight

quiz.q: A sensible weight for a pencil is…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “5 g”. Reasoning: Very light. A choice like “5 kg” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: A 1-litre bottle of water weighs about…
quiz.why: The correct answer is “1 kg”. Reasoning: Benchmark. A choice like “1 g” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “25 kg”. Reasoning: Typical range. A choice like “250 kg” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

scenes.text: Nani put 4 ladoos on each of 5 plates.

steps.title: Multiplication
steps.body:
Adding the **same number again and again** is multiplication.
4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = **5 × 4** = 20.
- 5 = number of groups, 4 = how many in each group, 20 = product.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 3 cycles, 2 wheels each → 2 + 2 + 2 = 3 × 2 = **6 wheels**.

**Example 2:** 6 + 6 + 6 + 6 = **4 × 6 = 24**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 3 + 4 + 5 as multiplication. Only **equal** groups can be multiplied.
- Confusing × (times) with + (plus).

steps.title: Order doesn't matter
steps.body: 5 × 4 = 4 × 5 = 20. If you know one, you know the other.

steps.title: Patterns that help

steps.body: Any number × 1 = the same number. Any number × 0 = 0.

courses.title: Ch 10 · Play with Patterns
courses.note: Chapter names follow the Math-Magic edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Shape patterns, number patterns, patterns made by turning, and secret codes.
outcomes: Learners can find the repeating unit in a pattern

scenes.text: Grandma knitted a border: red, red, blue, red, red, blue…
Ishaan spotted the repeating part: 'red, red, blue' — the core of the pattern.

steps.title: Core of a pattern
steps.body: A **repeating pattern** has a small part (the **core**) that repeats again and again. Find the core, then continue it.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** ⭐🌙🌙⭐🌙🌙⭐ … Core = ⭐🌙🌙. Next two = 🌙🌙.

**Example 2:** A B B C A B B C … What is the 9th letter? Core has 4 letters; 9th = 1st of the 3rd core = **A**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Choosing a core that is too short (just 'red, blue' in red-red-blue).
- Not checking the core over the whole pattern.

steps.title: Try it
steps.body: Make a pattern with spoons and forks on the table. Ask someone to find your core.

activity.prompt: Continue the pattern

steps.title: Turning
steps.body: Some patterns are made by **turning** a shape by the same amount each time — for example a **quarter turn** (like a clock hand moving from 12 to 3). After 4 quarter turns, the shape is back where it started.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** → ↓ ← ↑ → … (quarter turns clockwise). Next = **↓**.

**Example 2:** An arrow turns half a turn each time: → ← → ← … Next after ← is **→**.

steps.title: Common mistakes

scenes.text: Mamu made lassi in a big jug. He poured it into glasses.

steps.title: Capacity
steps.body: **Capacity** is how much a container can hold. We can compare by pouring: the container that fills **more cups** holds more.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Bottle A fills 4 cups, bottle B fills 7 cups. **B** holds more, by 7 − 4 = **3 cups**.

**Example 2:** A bucket fills 10 mugs. Two buckets fill 10 + 10 = **20 mugs**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking a tall thin glass always holds more than a short wide one. Pour and check!
- Comparing using different-size cups.

statements.s: A tall glass always holds more than a short glass.
To compare fairly, use the same cup each time.
Capacity tells how much a container can hold.

quiz.why: The correct answer is “How much it holds”. Reasoning: Definition. A choice like “How long” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

quiz.q: Jug A = 5 glasses, Jug B = 8 glasses. More?

steps.title: Standard units
steps.body:
- **Litre (L)** for bigger amounts: milk, petrol, a water bottle.
- **Millilitre (mL)** for small amounts: medicine, a spoon of oil.
- **1 L = 1000 mL**. Half litre = 500 mL. Quarter litre = 250 mL.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 3 L = **3000 mL**.

**Example 2:** 500 mL + 250 mL + 250 mL = 1000 mL = **1 L**.

**Example 3:** A teaspoon holds about 5 mL. 4 teaspoons = **20 mL**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Writing 1 L = 100 mL. It is **1000 mL**.
- Using litres for medicine doses.

steps.title: Medicine safety
steps.body: Medicine is measured in mL. Always let a grown-up measure it with the cup or syringe that comes with it.

steps.title: Use what you know
steps.body: Add, subtract, multiply — just like lengths and weights. Keep the **same unit**.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 20 L cooler, 5 L bucket → 4 buckets (5 × 4 = 20).

**Example 2:** A 1 L bottle; Amit drinks 350 mL. Left = 1000 − 350 = **650 mL**.

**Example 3:** Which is more: 1 L 200 mL or 1500 mL? 1 L 200 mL = 1200 mL, so **1500 mL** is more.

steps.title: Water in daily life
steps.body: We use water for drinking, cooking, bathing, cleaning and farming. Measuring water use helps us **save** it.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** A dripping tap wastes 5 L a day. In a week: 5 × 7 = **35 L**.

**Example 2:** Bathing with a bucket uses about 20 L; a long shower may use much more. Using a bucket saves water.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Thinking a few drops don't matter. Small leaks add up to many litres.

steps.title: Water audit
steps.body: With an adult, count how many 1 L bottles of water your family drinks in a day.

The correct answer is “Waste a lot”. Reasoning: They add up. A choice like “Are healthy” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “L and mL”. Reasoning: Capacity units. A choice like “m and cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “35 L”. Reasoning: 5 × 7. A choice like “25 L” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.why: The correct answer is “1000”. Reasoning: Fact. A choice like “10” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “mL”. Reasoning: Small amounts. A choice like “L” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Capacity is how much a container…
questions.why: The correct answer is “Holds”. Reasoning: Definition. A choice like “Weighs” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Jug fills 7 cups, mug fills 2 cups. Difference?
questions.why: The correct answer is “5 cups”. Reasoning: 7 − 2. A choice like “14 cups” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “250 mL”. Reasoning: 1000 ÷ 4. A choice like “25 mL” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “5000 mL”. Reasoning: 5 × 1000. A choice like “500 mL” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Water in a bucket is measured in…
questions.why: The correct answer is “L”. Reasoning: Large amount. A choice like “cm” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “250 mL”. Reasoning: 1000 − 750. A choice like “350 mL” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “2 L”. Reasoning: 2000 > 1800. A choice like “1800 mL” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: A 3 L bottle fills how many 500 mL glasses?
questions.why: The correct answer is “6”. Reasoning: 500 × 6 = 3000. A choice like “5” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.
The correct answer is “1 L”. Reasoning: 1000 mL. A choice like “1 L 400 mL” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: A family uses 15 L of drinking water a day. How much in a week?
questions.why: The correct answer is “105 L”. Reasoning: 15 × 7. A choice like “75 L” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Assertion: A tall thin glass may hold less than a short wide one. Reason: Capacity depends on both height and width.
questions.why: The correct answer is “Both true, R explains A”. Reasoning: Shape matters. A choice like “A false” may look tempting but does not fit what the question asks.

questions.q: Case: A 5 L can is full. Mummy pours out 1 L 250 mL and then 2 L 500 mL. How much is left?
questions.why: The correct answer is "1 L 250 mL". Poured 3 L 750 mL; 5000 − 3750 = 1250 mL. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Using only a 3 L jug and a 5 L jug, which amount can be measured by filling the 5 L jug and pouring it into the 3 L jug until full?
options: 2 L left in the 5 L jug
questions.why: The correct answer is "2 L left in the 5 L jug". 5 − 3 = 2 L remains. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

courses.title: Ch 12 · Can We Share?
courses.note: Chapter names follow the Math-Magic edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Division as equal sharing and as making equal groups, links with multiplication, and remainders.
outcomes: Learners can share objects equally
Learners can divide by making equal groups
Learners can use tables to divide
Learners can find what is left over (remainder)

scenes.text: Uncle gave 12 toffees to be shared among Asha, Babu and Chintu.
They gave one to each in turns until none were left. Each got 4. Fair!

steps.title: Division as sharing
steps.body:
**Dividing** means sharing into **equal** parts.
12 ÷ 3 = 4 means: 12 shared among 3 gives **4 each**.
- 12 = total, 3 = number of shares, 4 = each share.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 10 bananas for 2 monkeys → 10 ÷ 2 = **5 each**.

**Example 2:** 15 marbles among 5 friends → give one each round: after 3 rounds all 15 are given → **3 each**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Unequal sharing ('I get 5, you get 3') is not division.
- Mixing up the total and the number of shares.

activity.prompt: Tap all 12 toffees, then share them equally into 3 groups. How many in each group?

quiz.q: 8 sweets shared by 2 children. Each gets…
quiz.why: The correct answer is "4". 8 ÷ 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Equally". Equal parts. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "5". 4 × 5 = 20. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Number of shares". Divisor. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "3". 9 ÷ 3. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: A farmer has 24 eggs and trays that hold 6 eggs each.
He fills tray after tray: 6, 12, 18, 24. Four trays!

steps.title: Division as grouping
steps.body:
Division also answers: **how many groups** of a size can we make?
24 ÷ 6 = 4 means: 24 eggs make **4 trays** of 6.
You can find it by **repeated subtraction**: 24 − 6 − 6 − 6 − 6 = 0 (4 times).

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 30 children, teams of 5 → 30 ÷ 5 = **6 teams**.

**Example 2:** 21 − 7 = 14, 14 − 7 = 7, 7 − 7 = 0 → 3 subtractions, so 21 ÷ 7 = **3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Counting the subtractions wrongly. Tick each time you subtract.

activity.prompt: 36 pencils are packed in boxes of 4. How many boxes?

quiz.why: The correct answer is "8". 16 ÷ 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "4". Four tens in 40. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "4". Four subtractions. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "3". 18 ÷ 6. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Divide". Grouping. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Teacher asked, '35 ÷ 5?' Riya whispered the 5 table: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 35.
'Seven steps — the answer is 7!'

steps.title: Fact families
steps.body: If **5 × 7 = 35**, then **35 ÷ 5 = 7** and **35 ÷ 7 = 5**. Knowing tables makes division quick.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Thinking 5 ÷ 35 is the same as 35 ÷ 5. In division, **order matters**.
- Any number ÷ 1 = the same number; dividing by 0 is not allowed.

activity.prompt: Match each division with its answer

quiz.why: The correct answer is "4". Fact family. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "7". 9 × 7 = 63. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "7". 8 × 7 = 56. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Yes". 35 ÷ 5 ≠ 5 ÷ 35. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "17". Dividing by 1 keeps the number. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: 7 samosas for 3 friends. Each got 2, and 1 was left.
'We'll give the extra one to Dadi!' they decided.

steps.title: Remainder
steps.body:
Sometimes things cannot be shared equally. What is left over is the **remainder**.
7 ÷ 3 = 2, remainder 1. Check: 3 × 2 + 1 = 7.
The remainder is always **smaller** than the number we divide by.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 17 ÷ 5 → 5 × 3 = 15, 17 − 15 = 2 → **3 remainder 2**.

**Example 2:** 25 children, cars hold 4 each. 25 ÷ 4 = 6 remainder 1 → need **7 cars** so nobody is left behind!

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- A remainder equal to or bigger than the divisor means you can share one more round.
- In real-life problems, think about what the remainder means (an extra car is needed).

activity.prompt: Divide and find the remainder

quiz.why: The correct answer is "1". 2 × 5 = 10, 1 left. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Smaller than the divisor". Otherwise share again. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "4 r 2". 5 × 4 = 20, 2 left. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "3 × 4 + 2 = 14". Divisor × quotient + remainder. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "4". 10 ÷ 3 = 3 r 1, so one more boat. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.why: The correct answer is "3". Share 6 in 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Equal sharing". Definition. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "2". 5 × 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "7". Fact family. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "5". 6 × 5. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "5". 20 ÷ 4. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "1". 8 + 1. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "9". 8 × 9. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "6 r 2". 24 + 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which can be shared equally among 3 with nothing left?
questions.why: The correct answer is "27". 27 = 3 × 9. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "5". 5 subtractions. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Case: 50 laddoos are packed in boxes of 6. How many full boxes and how many left?
questions.why: The correct answer is "8 boxes, 2 left". 6 × 8 = 48; 2 left. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Assertion: In 23 ÷ 5 the remainder can be 6. Reason: The remainder must be less than the divisor.
questions.why: The correct answer is "A false, R true". 23 ÷ 5 = 4 r 3; 6 is not possible. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Case: 38 students go on a trip. Each van carries 8. How many vans are needed so all can go?
questions.why: The correct answer is "5". 38 ÷ 8 = 4 r 6 → 5 vans. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: A number divided by 7 gives 6 remainder 3. The number is…
questions.why: The correct answer is "45". 7 × 6 + 3 = 45. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

school-c3-maths-e.title: Class 3 Maths · Part E (Ch 13–14 + Revision)
school-c3-maths-e.description: Class 3 Mathematics: data handling with charts, money (rupees and paise), and a full-year revision with mock papers.

courses.title: Ch 13 · Smart Charts
courses.note: Chapter names follow the Math-Magic edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Collecting information, tally marks, tables, and simple pictographs; reading charts to answer questions.
outcomes: Learners can collect and record data with tally marks
Learners can make a simple table
Learners can read and draw a pictograph with a key
Learners can answer 'most', 'least' and 'how many more' questions from charts

scenes.text: Mr Paul asked each child, 'What is your favourite fruit?'
Kavya made a line for each answer. Every fifth line crossed the four before it — easy to count in fives!

steps.title: How to tally
steps.body: Draw one stroke | for each item. The **fifth** stroke goes across the first four: that bundle means **5**. Count bundles in fives, then add the loose strokes.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 2 bundles and 3 strokes = 5 + 5 + 3 = **13**.

**Example 2:** To show 8: one bundle of 5 and 3 strokes.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Drawing the fifth stroke as a separate line (then it is hard to count).
- Counting a bundle as 4.

activity.prompt: Mango: 3 bundles of five and 2 single strokes. How many children chose mango?

quiz.q: One tally bundle (4 strokes + 1 across) means…
quiz.why: The correct answer is "5". Five. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "14". 10 + 4. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: How do you show 7 in tally?
quiz.why: The correct answer is "1 bundle + 2 strokes". 5 + 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Count quickly". Easy counting in fives. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "20". 4 × 5. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Class 3 listed their pets: dogs 8, cats 5, fish 3, birds 4.
They put the numbers in a neat table on the wall.

steps.title: Reading a table
steps.body: A table has **rows and columns**. One column names things, another gives numbers. Read across a row to match a thing to its number.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Pets table:** Dog 8, Cat 5, Fish 3, Bird 4.

**Example 1:** Which pet is most common? The biggest number is 8 → **dog**.

**Example 2:** How many pets in all? 8 + 5 + 3 + 4 = **20**.

**Example 3:** How many more dogs than cats? 8 − 5 = **3**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Reading the number from the wrong row.
- For 'least', choosing the first item instead of the smallest number.

activity.prompt: Pets table: Dog 8, Cat 5, Fish 3, Bird 4
activity.text: The least common pet is ___. Dogs and birds together are ___.

quiz.q: Dog 8, Cat 5. How many more dogs?
quiz.why: The correct answer is "3". 8 − 5. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Dog". 8 is largest. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "20". Add all. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Fish". 3 < 4. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: In a table, a row usually shows…
quiz.why: The correct answer is "One item and its number". Item and value. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: The class drew a chart: one 📘 picture for every 2 books read.
Rahul's row had 4 📘 — so he read 8 books!

steps.title: Pictures that stand for numbers
steps.body: A **pictograph** uses pictures to show data. The **key** tells how much one picture stands for (e.g. 📘 = 2 books). Multiply pictures by the key.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
Key: 📘 = 2 books.

**Example 1:** Sara 📘📘📘 → 3 × 2 = **6 books**.

**Example 2:** To show 10 books, draw 10 ÷ 2 = **5 pictures**.

**Example 3:** Half a picture would stand for **1 book**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Ignoring the key and counting each picture as 1.
- Drawing pictures of different sizes (makes the chart confusing).

activity.prompt: Key: 🌳 = 5 trees. A village row shows 🌳🌳🌳🌳. How many trees?

quiz.why: The correct answer is "30". 3 × 10. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "6". 12 ÷ 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: The key in a pictograph tells…
quiz.why: The correct answer is "What one picture stands for". Value of a symbol. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "2". Half of 4. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "30". 6 × 5. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Survey: walk 12, bus 9, cycle 6, car 3.
The principal used the chart to decide where to build a new cycle stand.

steps.title: Using data to decide
steps.body: Data helps us answer questions and make decisions. Typical questions: *Which is the most? the least? How many more? How many in all?*

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Walkers vs car users: 12 − 3 = **9 more** walk.

**Example 2:** Children surveyed: 12 + 9 + 6 + 3 = **30**.

**Example 3:** Half the children walk? Half of 30 = 15; 12 walk, so **no**, fewer than half.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Answering 'how many more' with the total.
- Not reading the chart title, so missing what the numbers mean.

steps.title: Do a survey
steps.body: Ask 10 family members or friends their favourite colour. Make a tally, a table and a pictograph.

activity.prompt: Steps of doing a survey
items: Ask people and make tally marks

quiz.q: Walk 12, bus 9. How many more walk?
quiz.why: The correct answer is "3". 12 − 9. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Car". 3 is least. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "30". 12 + 9 + 6 + 3. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: First step of a survey is…
quiz.why: The correct answer is "Decide the question". Know what to ask. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Cycle 6 is how many times car 3?
quiz.why: The correct answer is "2 times". 6 = 2 × 3. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.why: The correct answer is "5". Five. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: In a pictograph the key tells…
questions.why: The correct answer is "Value of one picture". Key. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "6". 5 + 1. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "19". 15 + 4. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "10". 5 × 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Blue". 11 largest. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "22". Add. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "4". 40 ÷ 10. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Blue 11, Green 4. How many more chose Blue?
questions.why: The correct answer is "7". 11 − 4. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "10". 4 + 4 + 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Which is NOT a good survey question for a class?
options: How do you come to school?
questions.why: The correct answer is "Is 5 + 5 = 10?". That has one right answer, not data. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Case: Pictograph key 🍦 = 5. Monday 🍦🍦🍦, Tuesday 🍦🍦🍦🍦🍦. How many more ice-creams on Tuesday?
questions.why: The correct answer is "10". 25 − 15. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Assertion: If 🍎 = 3, then 6 apples need 2 pictures. Reason: 6 ÷ 3 = 2.
questions.why: The correct answer is "Both true, R explains A". Correct. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Case: 40 children were surveyed. Walk 15, bus 12, cycle ___, car 5. How many cycle?
questions.why: The correct answer is "8". 40 − 15 − 12 − 5 = 8. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

questions.q: Key 🌸 = 4. A row has 7 full 🌸 and half a 🌸. Number shown?
questions.why: The correct answer is "30". 7 × 4 = 28, plus 2. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

courses.title: Ch 14 · Rupees and Paise
courses.note: Chapter names follow the Math-Magic edition; topic order may differ by edition
courses.summary: Indian coins and notes, ₹1 = 100 paise, making amounts, adding money, giving change, and simple bills.
outcomes: Learners can name Indian coins and notes
Learners know ₹1 = 100 paise
Learners can make an amount using different notes and coins
Learners can add money, give change and read a bill

scenes.text: Mithu broke open his piggy bank on his birthday.
He found ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10 coins and a few ₹10 and ₹20 notes. He sorted them carefully.

steps.title: Indian money
steps.body:
- Money in India is the **rupee (₹)**.
- **₹1 = 100 paise**.
- Coins in common use: ₹1, ₹2, ₹5, ₹10, ₹20.
- Notes in common use: ₹10, ₹20, ₹50, ₹100, ₹200, ₹500.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** Mithu has 3 coins of ₹5 and 2 notes of ₹10. Total = 15 + 20 = **₹35**.

**Example 2:** 50 paise + 50 paise = 100 paise = **₹1**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Counting the number of coins instead of their value.
- Thinking ₹1 = 10 paise. It is **100 paise**.

steps.title: Fun fact
steps.body: The ₹ symbol was adopted in 2010. It is based on the Devanagari letter 'र' (ra) and the Roman letter R.

activity.prompt: You have two ₹20 notes, one ₹10 coin and three ₹2 coins. How much money?

quiz.why: The correct answer is "100". Hundred paise. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹20". 4 × 5. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

quiz.q: Which is a note in use today?
quiz.why: The correct answer is "₹500". Common note. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹25". Add. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
100 paise = ₹1, so 200 paise = ₹2.

scenes.text: An ice-cream costs ₹30. Pooja had a ₹20 note and two ₹5 coins.
Her brother paid with three ₹10 coins. Different coins, same ₹30!

steps.title: Same amount, different ways
steps.body: An amount can be made with different notes and coins. Start with the **biggest** note that fits, then make up the rest.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** ₹50 = ₹20 + ₹20 + ₹10, or 5 × ₹10, or one ₹50 note.

**Example 2:** Fewest notes/coins for ₹75: ₹50 + ₹20 + ₹5 = **3 pieces**.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body: - Using a note bigger than the amount when you need exact money.

activity.prompt: Match the amount with a way to make it

quiz.why: The correct answer is "₹20 + ₹20". 20 + 20. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹10 + ₹5". 2 pieces. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "10". 10 × 10. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹72". Add. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "four ₹5 coins". 4 × 5. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: A notebook cost ₹35. Sunil paid with a ₹50 note.
The shopkeeper counted up: 35 → 40 (₹5), 40 → 50 (₹10). 'Your change, ₹15!'

steps.title: Change
steps.body: **Change = money paid − cost.** Shopkeepers often **count up** from the cost to the money paid.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Subtracting the wrong way (35 − 50).
- Forgetting to check the change before leaving the shop.

steps.title: Be money smart
steps.body: Always count your change. If you are unsure, ask politely — it is fine to check.

activity.prompt: A pencil box costs ₹64. You pay with a ₹100 note. How much change?

quiz.why: The correct answer is "₹30". 50 − 20. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹5". 50 − 45. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹17". 83 → 100. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Paid − cost". Money given minus price. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹1". One rupee. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

scenes.text: Ammi's bill: Rice ₹120, Dal ₹95, Oil ₹150.

steps.title: A bill
steps.body: A **bill** lists each item, its **quantity**, its **rate** (price for one) and the **amount**. The **total** is the sum of all amounts.

steps.title: Solved examples
steps.body:
**Example 1:** 3 pens at ₹10 each = **₹30**; 2 erasers at ₹5 each = **₹10**. Total = **₹40**.

**Example 2:** Rice ₹120 + Dal ₹95 + Oil ₹150 = **₹365**. Paid ₹500 → change ₹135.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using the rate instead of the amount when there are many items.
- Adding numbers not lined up from the right.

activity.prompt: Complete the bill
activity.text: 4 notebooks at ₹15 each = ₹___. 2 pencils at ₹5 each = ₹___. Total = ₹___.

quiz.why: The correct answer is "₹20". 5 × 4. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹100". Add. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "Price of one item". Price per item. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹135". 500 − 365. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.
The correct answer is "₹90". 2 × 45. Check each of the other choices against this and you will see they do not fit the question.

courses.title: Class 3 Maths · Revision & Practice
courses.summary: All of Class 3 Maths on one page: key facts and methods, then two full mock papers and a mixed final test.
outcomes: Learners can recall every key fact of Class 3 Maths
Learners can solve mixed problems from all chapters
Learners can check answers and avoid common mistakes

scenes.text: Rhea made one big sheet with every fact she had learnt this year.
In the morning she read it once over breakfast and felt calm and ready.

steps.title: Numbers
steps.body:
- 10 ones = 1 ten; 10 tens = 1 hundred.
- Smallest 3-digit number 100, largest 999.
- Compare: hundreds first, then tens, then ones.
- Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6, 8.

steps.title: Operations
steps.body:
- Add and subtract from the **ones** column; carry/borrow.
- Check subtraction by adding.
- Multiplication = repeated addition; a × b = b × a; × 0 = 0; × 10 → add a zero.
- Division = equal sharing/grouping; remainder < divisor.

steps.title: Measurement and money
steps.body:
- 1 m = 100 cm · 1 kg = 1000 g · 1 L = 1000 mL · ₹1 = 100 paise.
- 1 week = 7 days · 1 year = 12 months · 1 hour = 60 minutes.
- Change = money paid − cost.

steps.title: Shapes and data
steps.body:
- Triangle 3 sides, square/rectangle 4 sides, circle no corners.
- Squares, rectangles, triangles and hexagons tile; circles leave gaps.
- Tally bundle = 5. Pictograph: pictures × key.

steps.title: Top 5 mistakes to avoid
steps.body:
- Forgetting the zero (305 not 35).
- Forgetting the carry.
- Subtracting smaller from bigger in each column.
- Mixing units (change to the same unit first).
- Ignoring the pictograph key.
